confidence_interval.rationale: The paper presents a conceptually novel idea (automatic gaze feature learning via CNN) with mixed empirical validation. Dataset 1 sentiment shows clear success (3.8% improvement, significant), but Dataset 2 sentiment shows failure (CNN underperforms handcrafted features), and sarcasm shows marginal benefit (1.36%, insignificant). The cross-dataset inconsistency is unexplained and raises fundamental questions about generalizability. The permutation invariance issue reveals an architectural limitation that deserves resolution. Methodologically, hyperparameter tuning by trial-and-error is insufficient for small datasets, and Dataset 2 overfitting (100% training, ~50% validation) suggests regularization is inadequate. The paper makes honest acknowledgments of limitations, which is commendable, but these limitations are substantial. The conceptual novelty is genuine and valuable, but the empirical case is not compelling enough to warrant strong acceptance. The work would benefit from resolving the cross-dataset inconsistency, addressing the permutation invariance issue, and providing more rigorous hyperparameter tuning. Confidence interval reflects genuine uncertainty about whether the approach generalizes beyond Dataset 1 sentiment analysis.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This paper proposes a CNN-based architecture for joint text-gaze feature learning in sentiment and sarcasm classification. The core claims are: (1) manual gaze feature extraction is insufficient for linguistic subtleties, (2) CNNs can automatically learn informative gaze features, (3) combined text+gaze CNNs outperform text-only CNNs and handcrafted systems. Cross-checking against manuscript evidence and prior work reveals a pattern of partially supported and overstated claims. Claim C1 (manual feature insufficiency) is motivational rather than empirically demonstrated—the 3.8% improvement on Dataset 1 is consistent with CNN being a better learner, not evidence of manual feature inadequacy. Claim C2 (CNN learns informative gaze features) relies on unvalidated analogy to image processing; no mechanistic explanation of learned filters is provided. Claim C3 (sentiment improvement) is contradicted by Dataset 2 results (CNN underperforms handcrafted features with 100% training accuracy and ~50% validation accuracy), suggesting overfitting rather than genuine learning. Claim C4 (sarcasm marginal benefit) contradicts the strong motivation in Section 2; the 1.36% improvement is statistically insignificant, raising questions about whether gaze is fundamentally less useful for sarcasm or dataset-specific. Claim C5 (fixation vs. saccade differences) is post-hoc interpretation without quantitative validation. Claim C6 (learned features interpretable) is based on qualitative visualization of 4 examples without quantitative distinctiveness metrics. The permutation invariance issue (Section 4.2, lines 476-499) represents a fundamental architectural violation: the P×G matrix representation assumes participant order independence, but the current implementation violates this by fixing participant order. The acknowledged workaround (all permutations) is computationally intractable. Retrieved literature on sentiment analysis (Kiritchenko et al. 2014) emphasizes the importance of feature engineering and lexicon-based approaches, which contextualizes the paper's claim that manual feature extraction is insufficient—the retrieved work shows handcrafted features can achieve competitive performance when well-designed. The paper's reasoning chain is logically coherent but empirically fragile: strong claims rest on Dataset 1 results, which are contradicted by Dataset 2 and undermined by acknowledged overfitting. The sarcasm task's minimal gaze benefit is particularly problematic, as it directly contradicts the motivational hypothesis that gaze captures pragmatic subtleties.

strengths.title: Novel multimodal fusion architecture for cognitive NLP
strengths.description: The dual-component CNN design (1D convolution for text, 2D convolution for gaze) represents a creative architectural contribution to the sparse domain of automatic gaze feature learning. The asymmetric design is conceptually motivated and well-articulated.

Figure 3: Clear visualization of architecture
Section 3: Motivation for CNN choice over alternatives

concerns.title: Claim C1 (manual feature insufficiency) is motivational rather than empirically demonstrated
concerns.description: The paper motivates the work by claiming manual gaze feature extraction is insufficient, but provides no direct empirical evidence. The 3.8% improvement on Dataset 1 is consistent with CNN being a better learner in general, not evidence that manual features are fundamentally insufficient. Retrieved literature (Kiritchenko et al. 2014) shows handcrafted features can achieve competitive performance when well-designed.

concerns.actionable_suggestion: Revise Claim C1 to acknowledge that manual features can be competitive when well-designed. Reframe the contribution as 'automatic feature learning as an alternative to manual engineering' rather than 'manual features are insufficient.' Add direct comparison of manual feature design quality across datasets.

concerns.title: Claim C2 (CNN learns informative gaze features) relies on unvalidated analogy to image processing
concerns.description: The paper argues CNNs should work for gaze data by analogy to image processing, but provides no mechanistic validation. No ablation isolates which learned filters correspond to claimed gaze attributes (saccades, fixations, progressions, regressions). The permutation invariance issue (Section 4.2) suggests 2D convolution may be fundamentally mismatched to gaze data.

Section 4.2, lines 476-499: Permutation invariance issue directly violates the assumption that gaze patterns are order-independent
No ablation study isolating learned filter meanings
Figure 4 visualization is qualitative and does not prove mechanistic informativeness
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add ablation study analyzing learned filters to identify which correspond to fixations, saccades, progressions, regressions. Compare CNN with alternative architectures (RNNs, attention) that may be more suitable for sequential gaze data. Address permutation invariance issue by either (a) proposing a scalable solution, (b) using a different architecture (e.g., RNN), or (c) acknowledging this as a fundamental limitation.

concerns.title: Cross-dataset inconsistency unexplained: Dataset 1 CNN advantage vs. Dataset 2 handcrafted advantage
concerns.description: Dataset 1 shows CNN outperforms handcrafted features (F=77.3 vs F=73.5), but Dataset 2 shows opposite trend (CNN F=62.0 vs handcrafted F=71.8). This fundamental inconsistency is acknowledged but not investigated. Without understanding why, generalization claims are premature.

Section 6.1, Table 1: Dataset 2 CNN disadvantage (9.8% worse than handcrafted)
Section 6.1, lines 501-599: Authors acknowledge overfitting on Dataset 2 but defer investigation to future work
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Investigate why Dataset 2 shows opposite trend. Possible explanations: (a) Dataset 2 is smaller (843 vs 994 snippets) and CNN overfits; (b) Dataset 2 has different linguistic properties; (c) Dataset 2 has fewer readers (5 vs 7) leading to noisier gaze data. Conduct analysis of dataset properties and gaze data quality. Consider whether Dataset 2 results invalidate the core hypothesis.

concerns.title: Severe overfitting on Dataset 2 (100% training, ~50% validation accuracy) undermines generalization claims
concerns.description: Dataset 2 shows training accuracy reaching 100% within 25 epochs with validation accuracy stable around 50%, indicating severe overfitting. This is acknowledged but not resolved; hyperparameter tuning is deferred to future work. The overfitting raises questions about whether Dataset 1 improvements are due to genuine learning or overfitting.

Section 5, lines 401-499: Hyperparameters set by trial-and-error; tuning deferred to future work
Dataset 2 is small (843 snippets); insufficient for CNN training without strong regularization
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Apply systematic hyperparameter tuning to Dataset 2, focusing on regularization (dropout, L2 norm constraints). Consider early stopping based on validation accuracy. If overfitting persists, acknowledge that CNN may not be suitable for small datasets without additional techniques (e.g., data augmentation, transfer learning). Investigate whether Dataset 1 results are also affected by overfitting.

concerns.title: Claim C4 (sarcasm marginal benefit) contradicts strong motivation in Section 2
concerns.description: Section 2 motivates the work by arguing gaze captures pragmatic subtleties in sarcasm, but Section 6.2 shows gaze adds only 1.36% improvement (statistically insignificant). This fundamental contradiction is not investigated. Why does gaze fail for sarcasm despite strong theoretical motivation?

Section 6.2, lines 601-699: 'improvement by adding gaze component is just 1.36%, which is statistically insignificant'
Section 6.2, lines 601-699: Authors note 'clear difference between the vocabulary of sarcasm and non-sarcasm classes' but do not investigate why gaze fails
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Investigate why gaze is less useful for sarcasm. Possible explanations: (a) sarcasm dataset has clear vocabulary distinction, making text sufficient; (b) gaze patterns for sarcasm are noisy or inconsistent across readers; (c) sarcasm requires pragmatic reasoning beyond what gaze captures. Conduct analysis of gaze data quality and consistency for sarcasm examples. Consider whether the strong motivation for gaze-based sarcasm detection is empirically justified.

concerns.title: Permutation invariance issue (Section 4.2) represents fundamental architectural violation
concerns.description: The paper acknowledges that the P×G matrix representation is not invariant to participant order: 'The gaze component of our network is not invariant of the order in which the scanpath data is given as input.' The acknowledged workaround (all permutations) is computationally intractable. The current practice (fixed participant order) violates the assumption that gaze patterns are order-independent.
evidence: Section 4.2, lines 476-499: 'The gaze component of our network is not invariant of the order in which the scanpath data is given as input'

Section 4.2, lines 476-499: 'The only way we can think of for addressing this issue is by applying convolution operations to all P × G matrices formed with all the permutations of P, capturing every possible ordering. Unfortunately, this makes the training process significantly less scalable'
Section 4.2, lines 476-499: 'As of now, training and testing are carried out by keeping the order of the input constant'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Acknowledge permutation invariance as a fundamental architectural limitation. Consider alternative architectures that are permutation-invariant: (a) RNNs with attention (order-independent via attention weights); (b) Set-based architectures (e.g., DeepSets); (c) Aggregation methods (e.g., mean/max pooling over participants before convolution). If CNN is retained, justify why fixed participant order is acceptable for the application.

concerns.title: Claim C5 (fixation vs. saccade differences) is post-hoc interpretation without quantitative validation
concerns.description: Section 7 claims saccade patterns are more informative than fixation for sentiment, but provides no statistical test of this difference. The explanation is post-hoc interpretation: 'saccade channel seems to be handing text having semantic incongruity better. Fixation channel does not help much, may be because of higher variance in fixation duration.' The variance claim is not quantified.
evidence: Section 7, lines 601-699: 'For sentiment detection, saccade channel seems to be handing text having semantic incongruity better. Fixation channel does not help much, may be because of higher variance in fixation duration.'
No statistical test comparing fixation and saccade contributions
Variance claim about fixation duration not quantified
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add quantitative analysis: (a) compute variance of fixation duration and saccade position across participants; (b) perform statistical test (e.g., t-test) comparing fixation and saccade channel contributions; (c) analyze correlation between gaze attributes and sentiment/sarcasm labels. This will validate or refute the post-hoc explanation.

concerns.title: Claim C6 (learned features interpretable) based on qualitative visualization of 4 examples without quantitative metrics
concerns.description: Figure 4 shows feature vectors as color-bars for only 4 sarcasm examples. The interpretation of color intensity as 'intensified negative opinion' is speculative. No quantitative metric of feature distinctiveness (e.g., separability, mutual information) is provided. Example 4 is misclassified by both systems, suggesting gaze does not help when context is insufficient.

No quantitative distinctiveness metrics

Show more examples (at least 10-20) to validate generalizability of visual patterns.

concerns.title: Hyperparameter tuning by trial-and-error without systematic validation
concerns.description: Section 5 states: 'These model hyper-parameters are fixed by trial and error and are possibly good enough to provide a first level insight into our system. Tuning of hyperparameters might help in improving the performance of our framework, which is on our future research agenda.' This is insufficient for empirical claims. concerns.title: Small datasets (994 and 843 snippets) with limited statistical power
concerns.description: Dataset 1 has 994 snippets with 7 readers per snippet; Dataset 2 has 843 snippets with 5 readers per snippet. These are small for CNN training. Sarcasm improvement (1.36%) is explicitly insignificant. No confidence intervals or variance estimates reported. Cross-validation with 10 folds on small data may exhibit high variance.

concerns.title: No comparison with alternative multimodal fusion methods or architectures
concerns.description: The paper proposes CNN-based fusion but does not compare with alternative approaches: late fusion, attention mechanisms, RNNs, or other multimodal architectures. This limits assessment of whether CNN is optimal for gaze data.

uncertainty_flags: Claim C1 (manual feature insufficiency) is motivational rather than empirically demonstrated. The 3.8% improvement on Dataset 1 is consistent with CNN being a better learner, not evidence of manual feature inadequacy. Dataset 2 results contradict this claim.

Claim C2 (CNN learns informative gaze features) relies on unvalidated analogy to image processing. No mechanistic explanation of learned filters. Permutation invariance issue suggests 2D convolution may be fundamentally mismatched to gaze data.
Claim C3 (sentiment improvement) is contradicted by Dataset 2 results (CNN underperforms handcrafted features). Cross-dataset inconsistency is unexplained and undermines generalization claims.
Claim C4 (sarcasm marginal benefit) contradicts strong motivation in Section 2. Why does gaze fail for sarcasm despite theoretical motivation? Is this task-dependent or dataset-dependent?
Claim C5 (fixation vs. saccade differences) is post-hoc interpretation without quantitative validation. Variance claim about fixation duration not quantified.
Claim C6 (learned features interpretable) is based on qualitative visualization of 4 examples. No quantitative distinctiveness metrics. Interpretation of color intensity is speculative.
Claim C7 (CNN outperforms on sarcasm) is primarily due to text component; gaze adds only 1.36%. Claim title emphasizes CNN advantage but gaze contribution is marginal.
Claim C8 (Dataset 2 overfitting) is acknowledged but not resolved. Hyperparameter tuning deferred to future work. Raises question: are Dataset 1 improvements due to genuine learning or overfitting?
Permutation invariance issue (Section 4.2) directly violates the assumption that gaze patterns are order-independent. Current practice (fixed participant order) is a fundamental architectural flaw.
Small datasets (994 and 843 snippets) with high variance across folds. Statistical power is limited; sarcasm improvement (1.36%) is explicitly insignificant.
No comparison with alternative architectures (RNNs, attention, late fusion). CNN may not be optimal for sequential gaze data.
Hyperparameters set by trial-and-error without systematic validation. Dataset 2 overfitting suggests regularization parameters are inadequate.
No investigation of why Dataset 2 shows opposite trend (CNN disadvantage) compared to Dataset 1. Generalization claims are premature.
Gaze data from 5-7 readers per snippet is small. No discussion of reader representativeness or individual differences in reading behavior.
Fixation duration and position are the only gaze attributes used. Other attributes (pupil dilation, blink rate) not explored or justified as unnecessary.
alternative_interpretations: The 3.8% improvement on Dataset 1 sentiment may reflect CNN's general superiority as a learner on small datasets, not evidence that manual gaze features are insufficient. Handcrafted features may be suboptimally engineered rather than fundamentally insufficient.

Dataset 2 overfitting (100% training, ~50% validation) may indicate that CNN is not suitable for small datasets without additional techniques (data augmentation, transfer learning, stronger regularization). The Dataset 1 improvements may also be affected by overfitting.

The marginal gaze benefit for sarcasm (1.36%, insignificant) may indicate that gaze is fundamentally less useful for sarcasm, or it may be dataset-specific. The sarcasm dataset's clear vocabulary distinction may make text sufficient, reducing gaze utility.

The permutation invariance issue may be a fundamental architectural flaw that invalidates the entire gaze component. Alternative architectures (RNNs, attention, set-based methods) may be more appropriate for gaze data.

The cross-dataset inconsistency (Dataset 1 CNN advantage vs. Dataset 2 handcrafted advantage) may reflect differences in dataset properties (size, linguistic characteristics, gaze data quality) rather than fundamental differences in method effectiveness.

The feature visualization (Figure 4) may show spurious patterns rather than genuine learned representations. The interpretation of color intensity as 'intensified opinion' is speculative and not validated quantitatively.

The paper's core hypothesis—that gaze captures pragmatic subtleties in sentiment and sarcasm—may be partially incorrect. Gaze may be useful for sentiment but not sarcasm, or vice versa, suggesting task-dependent utility rather than universal benefit.
transparency_notes: This review prioritizes evidence-based claim verification over binary accept/reject judgment. Each claim is cross-checked against manuscript evidence, prior work, and retrieved literature.
Uncertainty flags are explicitly separated from confirmed findings. Claims are categorized as supported, partially supported, or overstated based on available evidence.
The permutation invariance issue is treated as a fundamental architectural concern, not a minor limitation. The paper acknowledges this but does not resolve it, which is a critical gap.

Dataset 2 overfitting is treated as a major concern because it directly contradicts the core hypothesis and raises questions about Dataset 1 results. The paper acknowledges overfitting but defers investigation to future work.

The cross-dataset inconsistency is treated as a major concern because it undermines generalization claims. Without understanding why Dataset 2 shows opposite trend, the paper's conclusions are premature.
The sarcasm marginal benefit (1.36%, insignificant) is treated as contradicting the strong motivation in Section 2. This fundamental contradiction is not investigated in the paper.

Hyperparameter tuning by trial-and-error is treated as a methodological flaw because it is insufficient for empirical claims on small datasets. The paper acknowledges this but defers systematic tuning to future work.
Feature visualization (Figure 4) is treated as qualitative and speculative, not mechanistic validation. The interpretation of color intensity is post-hoc and not quantitatively validated.

The analogy to image processing (Section 3) is treated as suggestive but unvalidated. No mechanistic explanation of learned filters is provided, and the permutation invariance issue suggests the analogy may be flawed.

Retrieved literature (Kiritchenko et al. 2014) is used to contextualize the claim that manual feature extraction is insufficient. The retrieved work shows handcrafted features can achieve competitive performance when well-designed.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The paper occupies a sparse conceptual space—automatic gaze feature learning for NLP is genuinely underexplored. The dual-component CNN architecture (1D text, 2D gaze) is creative and represents a novel contribution to cognitive NLP. However, novelty does not guarantee validity. The empirical validation is mixed (Dataset 1 success, Dataset 2 failure, sarcasm marginal benefit), and fundamental architectural issues (permutation invariance) suggest the approach may be flawed. The creativity of the idea should not be conflated with the soundness of the execution.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If the permutation invariance issue were resolved (e.g., via RNN or set-based architecture), the gaze component would be more theoretically sound.
If Dataset 2 overfitting were addressed through systematic hyperparameter tuning, the cross-dataset inconsistency might be resolved, strengthening generalization claims.
If the sarcasm marginal benefit were investigated and explained (e.g., via analysis of gaze data quality or linguistic properties), the core hypothesis would be better validated.
If alternative architectures (RNNs, attention, late fusion) were compared, the paper could justify why CNN is optimal for gaze data.
If the paper directly compared manual feature sufficiency (e.g., by analyzing which manual features are most informative), Claim C1 would be empirically grounded.
If the paper reported confidence intervals and variance estimates, the statistical reliability of results would be clearer.
If the paper conducted cross-dataset validation (e.g., train on Dataset 1, test on Dataset 2), generalization would be more convincingly demonstrated.

This is a straightforward extension of existing CNN paradigms to a new modality. The novelty is bounded by reliance on standard CNN components and lack of architectural innovation beyond combining two convolution operations.

confidence_interval.rationale: The paper makes a reasonable conceptual contribution to cognitive NLP by proposing automatic gaze feature learning. However, empirical validation is mixed and methodologically flawed. Dataset 1 sentiment shows statistically significant improvement (supporting the core hypothesis), but Dataset 2 shows opposite trend (contradicting generalization), sarcasm shows marginal insignificant benefit (contradicting motivation), and severe overfitting on Dataset 2 raises questions about result reliability. Fundamental architectural issues (permutation invariance) and methodological gaps (hyperparameter tuning by trial-and-error, small datasets) further reduce confidence. The paper's contributions are meaningful but limited in scope and generalizability. Confidence is higher for the specific Dataset 1 sentiment result (high confidence) but lower for general claims about gaze utility and CNN suitability (low-medium confidence).

consensus_findings: The paper proposes a dual-component CNN architecture (1D text convolution, 2D gaze convolution) for joint text-gaze feature learning in sentiment and sarcasm classification. This architectural design is novel and well-motivated, representing a creative approach to multimodal fusion in cognitive NLP.

Dataset 1 sentiment analysis shows statistically significant improvement: 3.8% F-score over handcrafted baselines (77.3 vs 73.5) and 5% over text-only CNN (77.3 vs 72.35), confirmed by McNemar test (p < 0.05). This is the paper's strongest empirical result.

Dataset 2 sentiment analysis shows opposite trend: CNN underperforms handcrafted features (F=62.0 vs F=71.8), with severe overfitting (100% training accuracy, ~50% validation accuracy within 25 epochs). This cross-dataset inconsistency is acknowledged but unexplained.

Sarcasm detection shows marginal, statistically insignificant gaze benefit (1.36% improvement), contradicting the strong motivation in Section 2 that gaze captures pragmatic subtleties. The paper does not investigate why gaze is less useful for sarcasm than sentiment.

The permutation invariance issue (Section 4.2, lines 476-499) represents a fundamental architectural limitation: the P×G matrix representation assumes participant order independence, but the current implementation violates this by fixing participant order. The acknowledged workaround (all permutations) is computationally intractable.

Hyperparameter tuning is performed by trial-and-error without systematic validation. The authors acknowledge this is 'possibly good enough to provide a first level insight' but defer proper tuning to future work. Dataset 2 overfitting suggests regularization parameters are inadequate.

The paper uses small datasets (Dataset 1: 994 snippets with 7 readers; Dataset 2: 843 snippets with 5 readers) with 10-fold cross-validation and 10% validation split. No confidence intervals or variance estimates across folds are reported, limiting assessment of result reliability.

Feature interpretability claims (Claim C6) are based on qualitative visualization of 4 examples (Figure 4) without quantitative metrics of feature distinctiveness. The interpretation of color intensity as 'intensified negative opinion' is speculative and post-hoc.

The motivational claim that manual gaze feature extraction is insufficient (Claim C1) is not empirically demonstrated in the paper. The 3.8% improvement on Dataset 1 is consistent with CNN being a better learner in general, not evidence of manual feature inadequacy. Dataset 2 results contradict this claim.

No comparison with alternative multimodal fusion methods (late fusion, attention mechanisms, RNNs) is provided. The CNN analogy to image processing is suggestive but unvalidated for gaze data, and no ablation isolates which learned filters correspond to claimed gaze attributes (saccades, fixations, progressions, regressions).
disagreements: Reviewer 1 (structure_analyst) emphasizes logical coherence concerns and identifies the permutation invariance issue as a fundamental architectural flaw that undermines the entire gaze component. Reviewer 4 (novelty_assessor_disruptive) acknowledges the conceptual novelty but treats the permutation invariance issue as a resolvable technical limitation rather than a fundamental flaw. The disagreement centers on whether the issue is fatal or addressable.

Reviewer 3 (novelty_assessor_incremental) characterizes the contribution as incremental architectural engineering with limited methodological innovation. Reviewer 4 (novelty_assessor_disruptive) treats the automatic gaze feature learning as conceptually novel and underexplored, warranting higher novelty assessment. The disagreement reflects different novelty lenses: incremental vs. disruptive.

Reviewer 2 (methodology_auditor) treats Dataset 2 overfitting as evidence of fundamental unsuitability of CNN for small datasets. Reviewer 4 (novelty_assessor_disruptive) suggests Dataset 2 overfitting may be due to suboptimal hyperparameter tuning rather than architectural limitations, and that proper regularization could resolve the issue. The disagreement centers on whether overfitting is a fundamental or resolvable problem.

Reviewer 1 (structure_analyst) emphasizes that the sarcasm marginal benefit (1.36%, insignificant) directly contradicts the core hypothesis and undermines the entire motivation. Reviewer 4 (novelty_assessor_disruptive) treats this as a task-dependent limitation that does not invalidate the approach for sentiment analysis. The disagreement reflects different interpretations of task-specificity.

Reviewer 5 (claim_verifier) emphasizes that Claim C1 (manual feature insufficiency) is motivational rather than empirically demonstrated, and that Dataset 2 results contradict this claim. Reviewer 4 (novelty_assessor_disruptive) acknowledges the motivation is not empirically grounded but treats this as a reframing issue rather than a fundamental flaw. The disagreement centers on the severity of the motivational gap.
uncertainty_hotspots: Cross-dataset inconsistency (Dataset 1 CNN advantage vs. Dataset 2 handcrafted advantage) is unexplained. Possible causes: (a) Dataset 2 is smaller and CNN overfits; (b) Dataset 2 has different linguistic properties; (c) hyperparameters are suboptimal for Dataset 2; (d) gaze data quality differs between datasets. Without investigation, generalization claims are premature.

Sarcasm marginal gaze benefit (1.36%, insignificant) contradicts strong motivation in Section 2. Possible explanations: (a) sarcasm dataset has clear vocabulary distinction, making gaze redundant; (b) gaze patterns for sarcasm are noisy or inconsistent; (c) sarcasm requires pragmatic reasoning beyond gaze; (d) dataset is unrepresentative of general sarcasm phenomena. The paper does not investigate which.

Permutation invariance issue (Section 4.2) violates the assumption that gaze patterns are order-independent. Possible interpretations: (a) fundamental architectural flaw that invalidates the gaze component; (b) resolvable through alternative architectures (RNNs, attention, set-based methods); (c) acceptable if participant order is consistent across training and testing. The paper acknowledges but does not resolve this.

Dataset 2 severe overfitting (100% training, ~50% validation) could indicate: (a) CNN is fundamentally unsuitable for small datasets; (b) hyperparameters are suboptimal and need tuning; (c) dataset size is insufficient for CNN training; (d) regularization strategy is inadequate. The paper acknowledges but defers investigation to future work.

Feature visualization (Figure 4) shows qualitative differences in 4 examples, but interpretation is speculative. Possible interpretations: (a) learned features genuinely capture interpretable differences; (b) visualization artifacts or cherry-picked examples; (c) differences are not statistically significant or generalizable. No quantitative validation provided.

Claim C1 (manual feature insufficiency) is motivational but not empirically demonstrated. Possible interpretations: (a) manual features are fundamentally insufficient; (b) manual features are suboptimally engineered in prior work; (c) CNN is a better learner in general, not because manual features are insufficient. Retrieved literature (Kiritchenko et al. 2014) shows handcrafted features can be competitive.

CNN analogy to image processing (Section 3) is unvalidated. Possible interpretations: (a) analogy is valid and CNN is appropriate for gaze data; (b) analogy is flawed because gaze is sequential and permutation-sensitive, unlike images; (c) alternative architectures (RNNs, attention) are more suitable. No mechanistic validation provided.

Hyperparameter tuning by trial-and-error could indicate: (a) hyperparameters are adequate for first-level insight; (b) hyperparameters are suboptimal and systematic tuning would improve results; (c) Dataset 2 overfitting is due to inadequate regularization. The paper defers systematic tuning to future work.

Small dataset sizes (994 and 843 snippets) with 5-7 readers per snippet could indicate: (a) datasets are sufficient for CNN training with proper regularization; (b) datasets are too small and CNN overfits; (c) reader pool is too small to capture population-level gaze patterns. No power analysis or reader representativeness analysis provided.

Gaze representation limited to fixation duration and position could indicate: (a) these are the most informative gaze attributes; (b) other attributes (pupil dilation, blink rate) are less informative; (c) other attributes are unexplored and potentially informative. No justification or ablation provided.
model_diversity_effects: Reviewer 1 (structure_analyst, logical-coherence-first) identifies logical fractures in the argument chain, particularly the contradiction between Dataset 1 success and Dataset 2 failure. This epistemic variant prioritizes coherence and identifies where the reasoning breaks down.

Reviewer 2 (methodology_auditor, reproducibility-and-validity-first) emphasizes methodological rigor and identifies hyperparameter tuning, overfitting, and small dataset size as critical concerns. This variant prioritizes empirical validity and reproducibility.

Reviewer 3 (novelty_assessor_incremental, incremental-contribution lens) characterizes the work as incremental architectural engineering with limited novelty relative to existing CNN and gaze-based sentiment analysis work. This variant emphasizes semantic overlap and existing paradigms.

Reviewer 4 (novelty_assessor_disruptive, disruptive-thinking lens) acknowledges conceptual novelty in automatic gaze feature learning and treats the work as underexplored. This variant emphasizes sparse precedent and innovation signal.

meta_review.editor_guidance: This paper presents a conceptually novel approach to automatic gaze feature learning for sentiment and sarcasm classification, with mixed empirical validation and significant methodological concerns. The core contribution—a dual-component CNN architecture for joint text-gaze feature learning—is creative and addresses a sparse domain (automatic gaze feature learning for NLP). However, the execution reveals fundamental architectural limitations (permutation invariance issue), methodological gaps (hyperparameter tuning by trial-and-error, small datasets), and inconsistent empirical results (Dataset 1 success, Dataset 2 failure, sarcasm marginal benefit). The paper makes honest acknowledgments of limitations but defers resolution to future work, which is insufficient for a strong contribution. Key decision points: (1) Is the permutation invariance issue a fatal architectural flaw or a resolvable limitation? (2) Does the cross-dataset inconsistency invalidate the core hypothesis or reflect dataset-specific factors? (3) Is the sarcasm marginal benefit evidence that gaze is fundamentally less useful for sarcasm, or is this dataset-specific? (4) Are the Dataset 1 improvements due to genuine learning or overfitting? The paper would be strengthened by: (a) resolving the permutation invariance issue through alternative architectures or theoretical justification; (b) investigating the cross-dataset inconsistency through analysis of dataset properties and hyperparameter tuning; (c) explaining why gaze is less useful for sarcasm; (d) addressing Dataset 2 overfitting through systematic hyperparameter tuning; (e) comparing with alternative multimodal fusion methods. Without these improvements, the contribution is incremental and the empirical case is not compelling. The paper is suitable for a workshop or specialized venue focused on cognitive NLP, but falls short of the rigor expected for a top-tier conference.
meta_review.author_guidance: Your paper makes a meaningful conceptual contribution to cognitive NLP by proposing automatic gaze feature learning via CNN. The Dataset 1 sentiment results are encouraging and statistically significant. However, several critical issues need resolution before publication: (1) Permutation invariance issue (Section 4.2): The P×G matrix representation violates the assumption that participant order is independent. The current workaround (fixed participant order) is ad-hoc. Consider alternative architectures (RNNs, attention, set-based methods) that are inherently permutation-invariant. (2) Cross-dataset inconsistency: Dataset 1 shows CNN advantage (77.3 vs 73.5), but Dataset 2 shows opposite trend (62.0 vs 71.8). Investigate why. Possible causes: dataset size, hyperparameter mismatch, gaze data quality, linguistic properties. Conduct cross-dataset validation (train on Dataset 1, test on Dataset 2). (3) Sarcasm marginal benefit (1.36%, insignificant): This contradicts the strong motivation in Section 2. Investigate why gaze is less useful for sarcasm. Analyze gaze patterns in sarcastic vs. non-sarcastic texts. Consider whether the sarcasm dataset is representative. (4) Dataset 2 overfitting (100% training, ~50% validation): Perform systematic hyperparameter tuning (grid search or Bayesian optimization) focusing on dropout and L2 regularization. Use early stopping based on validation loss. Report learning curves. (5) Hyperparameter tuning: Replace trial-and-error with systematic search. Report sensitivity analysis for key hyperparameters. Justify final choices. (6) Feature interpretability: Add quantitative metrics (feature importance, mutual information, separability) to support interpretability claims. Expand visualization to more examples (10-20+). (7) Statistical reporting: Report confidence intervals and variance estimates across folds. Provide p-values for all comparisons. Conduct power analysis given small dataset sizes. (8) Architectural comparison: Compare with alternative multimodal fusion methods (late fusion, attention, RNNs) to justify CNN choice. (9) Motivation validation: Empirically validate Claim C1 (manual feature insufficiency) by analyzing which manual features are most informative and why learned features are superior. (10) Gaze representation: Explore additional gaze attributes (pupil dilation, blink rate, saccade amplitude) and justify the choice of fixation duration and position. epistemic_limits: The paper's empirical validation is limited to two small datasets (994 and 843 snippets) with 5-7 readers per snippet. Generalization to larger datasets, other languages, and other domains is unclear.
The cross-dataset inconsistency (Dataset 1 CNN advantage vs. Dataset 2 handcrafted advantage) is unexplained. Without understanding why, it is impossible to determine when the approach is applicable.
The sarcasm marginal benefit (1.36%, insignificant) contradicts the strong motivation. It is unclear whether gaze is fundamentally less useful for sarcasm or whether this is dataset-specific.

The permutation invariance issue is acknowledged but unresolved. The current workaround (fixed participant order) violates the assumption that gaze patterns are order-independent. The implications for real-world deployment are unclear.
Hyperparameter tuning by trial-and-error is insufficient for determining optimal model configuration. Systematic tuning could substantially change results, particularly for Dataset 2.
Feature interpretability claims are based on qualitative visualization of 4 examples. Quantitative validation is lacking, and the interpretation is speculative.

The analogy between gaze data and images (Section 3) is unvalidated. It is unclear whether 2D convolution is appropriate for gaze data, or whether alternative architectures (RNNs, attention) would be more suitable.
The motivational claim that manual gaze feature extraction is insufficient is not empirically demonstrated. Dataset 2 results suggest handcrafted features may be superior in some cases.
The paper does not investigate why gaze is less useful for sarcasm than sentiment. This limits understanding of when gaze is beneficial and when it is not.
The paper does not analyze gaze data quality or reader representativeness. It is unclear whether 5-7 readers per snippet is sufficient to capture population-level gaze patterns.

The paper does not compare with alternative multimodal fusion methods. It is unclear whether CNN is optimal for gaze data, or whether RNNs, attention mechanisms, or late fusion would be more effective.
Small dataset sizes limit statistical power. The sarcasm improvement (1.36%) is explicitly insignificant, and confidence intervals are not reported for other results.

The paper does not provide mechanistic explanation of how learned filters correspond to gaze attributes (saccades, fixations, progressions, regressions). It is unclear what the CNN is actually learning from gaze data.
The paper does not investigate whether Dataset 1 improvements are due to genuine learning or overfitting. Dataset 2 overfitting raises questions about the reliability of Dataset 1 results.
The paper does not analyze which text-gaze feature combinations are most informative. All 9 variants are tested but not ranked by contribution or analyzed for interaction effects.

The core contribution is replacing handcrafted gaze features with automatically learned CNN features. Dataset 1 sentiment analysis shows statistically significant improvement (3.8% F-score over handcrafted baselines, p<0.05), but Dataset 2 shows opposite trend (CNN underperforms by 9.8%), and sarcasm shows marginal, insignificant benefit (1.36%). The work addresses a sparse domain (automatic gaze feature learning for NLP) and presents a creative architectural design, but suffers from fundamental limitations: (1) permutation invariance issue violates core architectural assumption with no scalable solution, (2) cross-dataset inconsistency unexplained, (3) hyperparameter tuning by trial-and-error without systematic validation, (4) severe Dataset 2 overfitting (100% training, ~50% validation), (5) sarcasm results contradict strong motivation. The paper makes honest acknowledgments of limitations but defers resolution to future work. Empirical validation is mixed and methodologically flawed, limiting confidence in generalizability.

limitations: Permutation invariance issue (Section 4.2, lines 476-499): P×G matrix representation assumes participant order independence, but implementation violates this by fixing participant order. Acknowledged workaround (all permutations) is computationally intractable. This is a fundamental architectural flaw with no scalable solution.

Cross-dataset inconsistency unexplained: Dataset 1 shows CNN advantage (F=77.3 vs F=73.5), but Dataset 2 shows opposite trend (F=62.0 vs F=71.8). Severe overfitting on Dataset 2 (100% training accuracy, ~50% validation accuracy within 25 epochs) suggests hyperparameter inadequacy. Without investigation, generalization claims are premature.

Is the permutation invariance issue a fatal architectural flaw or a resolvable limitation? Would alternative architectures (RNNs, attention, set-based methods) that are inherently permutation-invariant perform better? Comparison with these alternatives would justify CNN choice.

Are Dataset 1 improvements due to genuine learning or overfitting? Dataset 2 severe overfitting (100% training, ~50% validation) raises questions about Dataset 1 reliability. Systematic hyperparameter tuning and learning curve analysis would clarify.

source_trace: Mishra et al. (2016b,c): Primary baseline for handcrafted gaze-based sentiment/sarcasm classification. Dataset 1 sentiment best: F=73.5; sarcasm best: F=75.7. This paper's CNN achieves F=77.3 (sentiment Dataset 1) and F=86.97 (sarcasm), but Dataset 2 shows opposite trend (CNN F=62.0 vs handcrafted F=71.8).

Kim (2014): Foundational CNN architecture for text classification. This paper's text component is 'quite similar' to Kim (2014). Text-only CNN baseline: F=72.35 (sentiment Dataset 1). Gaze adds 5% improvement.

Kiritchenko et al. (2014): Sentiment analysis using handcrafted lexicon and surface features. Achieves F=70.45 on SemEval-2013. Demonstrates that well-designed handcrafted features can be competitive, contextualizing the claim that manual feature extraction is insufficient.

Rayner & Duffy (1986), Kutas & Hillyard (1980): Cognitive science literature on surprisal and cognitive load effects on eye-movement patterns. Cited in Section 2 to motivate gaze-based sentiment/sarcasm detection.

Krizhevsky et al. (2012): ImageNet CNNs for image processing. Cited in Section 3 to motivate CNN analogy to gaze data. However, analogy is unvalidated; gaze data has sequential and permutation-sensitive structure unlike images.
McNemar test (Section 6.1): Statistical significance test for paired classifier outputs. Applied to Dataset 1 sentiment comparison (p<0.05). Not applied to Dataset 2 or sarcasm comparisons.

Section 4.2, lines 476-499: Permutation invariance issue. Authors acknowledge P×G matrix representation is not invariant to participant order. Proposed workaround (all permutations) is computationally intractable. Current practice (fixed participant order) violates order-independence assumption.

Section 6.1, Table 1: Dataset 1 sentiment results. Best CNN variant (NONSTATICTEXT + MULTICHANNELGAZE): F=77.3 vs Mishra et al. (2016c) best: F=73.5 (3.8% improvement, p<0.05). Dataset 2 sentiment: CNN F=62.0 vs Mishra et al. (2016c) best: F=71.8 (9.8% underperformance).

Section 6.2, Table 2: Sarcasm results. Best CNN variant (MULTICHANNELTEXT + FIXATION): F=86.97 vs Mishra et al. (2016b) best: F=75.7 (11.27% improvement). However, gaze-only contribution: 1.36% (MULTICHANNELTEXT + FIXATION F=86.97 vs MULTICHANNELTEXT F=85.63), statistically insignificant.

Section 7, Figure 4: Feature visualization for 4 sarcasm examples. Qualitative interpretation of color-bar intensity as 'intensified negative opinion.' No quantitative distinctiveness metrics. Example 4 misclassified by both systems.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 6. Check that the tone is professional and neutral I4
Codes: I4
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: Above all, a good review should be professional and neutral, if not kind. A key goal of peer review is to help the authors improve their papers. As an anonymous reviewer, you are in a position of power, and the written medium makes it easier to be more dismissive and sarcastic than if you were communicating with the authors face-to-face. Unfortunately such reviews are not uncommon. Consider that you may well be addressing someone who is only starting on the research path. And/or someone struggling with stress and other mental health issues. And/or someone who has been less lucky with their school and advisors. Academic lives are already stressful enough, and we do not need to inflict extra damage on the mental health of our colleagues with sarcastic or insulting reviews. Write the review you would like to get yourself. The fact is, authors and reviewers are actually the same people: the conference crowd lining up for coffee, happily chatting with each other about the grand problems even if they do not always agree. Why can’t we do peer review in the same spirit of fun intellectual interaction with colleagues? Just like the conference coffee break chats, reviewing is in fact, mutually beneficial: in exchange for feedback, the reviewers get to have the first look at cutting-edge research. Just like the coffee breaks, where you do not necessarily meet only the people working in your subsubfield, peer review may expose you to new techniques.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 6. Check that the tone is professional and neutral I4
Codes: I4
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: Above all, a good review should be professional and neutral, if not kind. A key goal of peer review is to help the authors improve their papers. As an anonymous reviewer, you are in a position of power, and the written medium makes it easier to be more dismissive and sarcastic than if you were communicating with the authors face-to-face. Unfortunately such reviews are not uncommon. Consider that you may well be addressing someone who is only starting on the research path. And/or someone struggling with stress and other mental health issues. And/or someone who has been less lucky with their school and advisors. Academic lives are already stressful enough, and we do not need to inflict extra damage on the mental health of our colleagues with sarcastic or insulting reviews. Write the review you would like to get yourself. The fact is, authors and reviewers are actually the same people: the conference crowd lining up for coffee, happily chatting with each other about the grand problems even if they do not always agree. Why can’t we do peer review in the same spirit of fun intellectual interaction with colleagues? Just like the conference coffee break chats, reviewing is in fact, mutually beneficial: in exchange for feedback, the reviewers get to have the first look at cutting-edge research. Just like the coffee breaks, where you do not necessarily meet only the people working in your subsubfield, peer review may expose you to new techniques.

Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none

Content: cs committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct. There is already a policy on review incentives and sanctions, including temporary bans on (re-)submission or commitment to ACL venues. To add to the above points, the reviews that look like they were written by ChatGPT overall decrease the faith in the peer review process. According to this study, there is more generated text in ‘reviews which report lower confidence, were submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who are less likely to respond to author rebuttals’. All these factors generally correspond to the type of unmotivated reviewer that, as authors, we would prefer to avoid. The increased ratio of such reviews also attunes the community to reviews that sound like they were generated. Generally, reviews are valued for their content rather than language, so your thoughts are more likely to be appreciated if they come in your voice (even if with linguistic imperfections). Finally: some authors actually count on you to use generative AI, and include hidden prompt injections intended to manipulate your assistant into giving a positive review! If you notice anything like that, please raise it with the chairs, such submissions should be desk rejected. What about the authors, can they use generative AI? The ACL policy on publication ethics discusses various cases with different degrees of acceptability.

top_documents.title: Document 2
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 6. Check that the tone is professional and neutral I4
Codes: I4
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: Above all, a good review should be professional and neutral, if not kind. A key goal of peer review is to help the authors improve their papers. As an anonymous reviewer, you are in a position of power, and the written medium makes it easier to be more dismissive and sarcastic than if you were communicating with the authors face-to-face. Unfortunately such reviews are not uncommon. Consider that you may well be addressing someone who is only starting on the research path. And/or someone struggling with stress and other mental health issues. And/or someone who has been less lucky with their school and advisors. Academic lives are already stressful enough, and we do not need to inflict extra damage on the mental health of our colleagues with sarcastic or insulting reviews. Write the review you would like to get yourself. The fact is, authors and reviewers are actually the same people: the conference crowd lining up for coffee, happily chatting with each other about the grand problems even if they do not always agree. Why can’t we do peer review in the same spirit of fun intellectual interaction with colleagues? Just like the conference coffee break chats, reviewing is in fact, mutually beneficial: in exchange for feedback, the reviewers get to have the first look at cutting-edge research. Just like the coffee breaks, where you do not necessarily meet only the people working in your subsubfield, peer review may expose you to new techniques.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, policy_screen
Content: cs committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct. There is already a policy on review incentives and sanctions, including temporary bans on (re-)submission or commitment to ACL venues. To add to the above points, the reviews that look like they were written by ChatGPT overall decrease the faith in the peer review process. According to this study, there is more generated text in ‘reviews which report lower confidence, were submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who are less likely to respond to author rebuttals’. All these factors generally correspond to the type of unmotivated reviewer that, as authors, we would prefer to avoid. The increased ratio of such reviews also attunes the community to reviews that sound like they were generated. Generally, reviews are valued for their content rather than language, so your thoughts are more likely to be appreciated if they come in your voice (even if with linguistic imperfections). Finally: some authors actually count on you to use generative AI, and include hidden prompt injections intended to manipulate your assistant into giving a positive review! If you notice anything like that, please raise it with the chairs, such submissions should be desk rejected. What about the authors, can they use generative AI? The ACL policy on publication ethics discusses various cases with different degrees of acceptability.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 6. Check that the tone is professional and neutral I4
Codes: I4
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: Above all, a good review should be professional and neutral, if not kind. A key goal of peer review is to help the authors improve their papers. As an anonymous reviewer, you are in a position of power, and the written medium makes it easier to be more dismissive and sarcastic than if you were communicating with the authors face-to-face. Unfortunately such reviews are not uncommon. Consider that you may well be addressing someone who is only starting on the research path. And/or someone struggling with stress and other mental health issues. And/or someone who has been less lucky with their school and advisors. Academic lives are already stressful enough, and we do not need to inflict extra damage on the mental health of our colleagues with sarcastic or insulting reviews. Write the review you would like to get yourself. The fact is, authors and reviewers are actually the same people: the conference crowd lining up for coffee, happily chatting with each other about the grand problems even if they do not always agree. Why can’t we do peer review in the same spirit of fun intellectual interaction with colleagues? Just like the conference coffee break chats, reviewing is in fact, mutually beneficial: in exchange for feedback, the reviewers get to have the first look at cutting-edge research. Just like the coffee breaks, where you do not necessarily meet only the people working in your subsubfield, peer review may expose you to new techniques.

Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, policy_screen
Content: cs committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct. There is already a policy on review incentives and sanctions, including temporary bans on (re-)submission or commitment to ACL venues. To add to the above points, the reviews that look like they were written by ChatGPT overall decrease the faith in the peer review process. According to this study, there is more generated text in ‘reviews which report lower confidence, were submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who are less likely to respond to author rebuttals’. All these factors generally correspond to the type of unmotivated reviewer that, as authors, we would prefer to avoid. The increased ratio of such reviews also attunes the community to reviews that sound like they were generated. Generally, reviews are valued for their content rather than language, so your thoughts are more likely to be appreciated if they come in your voice (even if with linguistic imperfections). Finally: some authors actually count on you to use generative AI, and include hidden prompt injections intended to manipulate your assistant into giving a positive review! If you notice anything like that, please raise it with the chairs, such submissions should be desk rejected. What about the authors, can they use generative AI? The ACL policy on publication ethics discusses various cases with different degrees of acceptability.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 6. Check that the tone is professional and neutral I4
Codes: I4
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: Above all, a good review should be professional and neutral, if not kind. A key goal of peer review is to help the authors improve their papers. As an anonymous reviewer, you are in a position of power, and the written medium makes it easier to be more dismissive and sarcastic than if you were communicating with the authors face-to-face. Unfortunately such reviews are not uncommon. Consider that you may well be addressing someone who is only starting on the research path. And/or someone struggling with stress and other mental health issues. And/or someone who has been less lucky with their school and advisors. Academic lives are already stressful enough, and we do not need to inflict extra damage on the mental health of our colleagues with sarcastic or insulting reviews. Write the review you would like to get yourself. The fact is, authors and reviewers are actually the same people: the conference crowd lining up for coffee, happily chatting with each other about the grand problems even if they do not always agree. Why can’t we do peer review in the same spirit of fun intellectual interaction with colleagues? Just like the conference coffee break chats, reviewing is in fact, mutually beneficial: in exchange for feedback, the reviewers get to have the first look at cutting-edge research. Just like the coffee breaks, where you do not necessarily meet only the people working in your subsubfield, peer review may expose you to new techniques.

Content: cs committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct. To add to the above points, the reviews that look like they were written by ChatGPT overall decrease the faith in the peer review process. According to this study, there is more generated text in ‘reviews which report lower confidence, were submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who are less likely to respond to author rebuttals’. All these factors generally correspond to the type of unmotivated reviewer that, as authors, we would prefer to avoid. The increased ratio of such reviews also attunes the community to reviews that sound like they were generated. Generally, reviews are valued for their content rather than language, so your thoughts are more likely to be appreciated if they come in your voice (even if with linguistic imperfections). Finally: some authors actually count on you to use generative AI, and include hidden prompt injections intended to manipulate your assistant into giving a positive review! The ACL policy on publication ethics discusses various cases with different degrees of acceptability.

Mohammad Saif.Mohammad@nrc-cnrc.gc.ca National Research Council Canada 1200 Montreal Rd., Ottawa, ON, Canada Abstract We describe a state-of-the-art sentiment analysis system that detects (a) the sentiment of short informal textual messages such as tweets and SMS (message-level task) and (b) the sentiment of a word or a phrase within a message (term-level task). The system is based on a supervised statistical text classiﬁcation approach leveraging a variety of surface- form, semantic, and sentiment features. The sentiment features are primarily derived from novel high-coverage tweet-speciﬁc sentiment lexicons. These lexicons are automatically generated from tweets with sentiment-word hashtags and from tweets with emoticons. To adequately capture the sentiment of words in negated contexts, a separate sentiment lexicon is generated for negated words. The system ranked ﬁrst in the SemEval-2013 shared task ‘Sentiment Analysis in Twit- ter’ (Task 2), obtaining an F-score of 69.02 in the message-level task and 88.93 in the term-level task. Post-competition improvements boost the performance to an F-score of 70.45 (message-level task) and 89.50 (term-level task). The system also obtains state-of- the-art performance on two additional datasets: the SemEval-2013 SMS test set and a corpus of movie review excerpts. The ablation experiments demonstrate that
